summary: Mobile IPv6 devices need to know their home agent and home network. This RFC defines DHCP options that let a mobile node ask for the home agent address, its fully qualified domain name, or the home network prefix, and get the answer in the DHCP reply.

plainLanguage.summary: A traveling kid needs to know the phone number of home. This lets the kid just ask the helper at the front desk, who tells them.

subtitle: DHCPv6 options that tell a Mobile IPv6 device which home agent and home network to use.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 node must know its home agent before it can do any Mobile IPv6 signaling, but the standard discovery scheme only works if the node already knows the home network prefix.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines seven new DHCPv6 options that carry a home network prefix, a home agent IP address or a home agent FQDN, so the node can ask for them in a normal DHCP exchange.
tldr.outcome: A roaming node can bootstrap from DHCP alone. The options add no new security of their own, because the node and its home agent authenticate each other directly.

today: RFC 6610 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. RFC 6611 builds on these options for the integrated bootstrapping scenario.

sections.title: Finding a Home Agent Without a Prefix
sections.content:
Before a mobile node can do Mobile IPv6 signaling, it needs the address of a home agent. It can be pre-configured, or discovered dynamically. The Mobile IPv6 specification (RFC 6275) describes dynamic discovery, but only for nodes that already know the home network prefix. That fails when the prefix is not available.

This RFC extends DHCPv6 (RFC 3315, RFC 3736) so that the server can deliver the home agent's IP address or its Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN). It can also deliver the home prefix, which the node may then use for the dynamic discovery in RFC 6275.

The node does not have to be attached to its home network when it asks. A node that is already roaming can obtain the bootstrap parameters from its home network, and operators can deploy home agents centrally. The same need arises with Hierarchical Mobile IPv6, where the node must find a MAP (a special home agent) several hops away.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are lost, you need to know where home is. This memo gives the helper a way to tell you, even when you do not know your own street name.

sections.title: The Seven New Options
sections.content:
The options all start with MIPv6 in their names, but the RFC drops that prefix in its prose. They fall into three groups.

  • Home Network ID FQDN (code 49): an FQDN naming the home network the client wants information about. A server also uses it inside an Identified Home Network Information option to say which network the answer is for.
  • Home Network Information options: three wrappers that each hold one or more other options. Visited (50) describes the local home network in the visited domain, Identified (69) describes the network named by a Home Network ID FQDN, and Unrestricted (70) describes a network chosen by the server administrator.
  • Content options: Home Network Prefix (71, with a prefix length and the prefix), Home Agent Address (72) and Home Agent FQDN (73). Each should appear only inside one of the Home Network Information options.

The Home Agent Address option may hold an IPv4 address written as an IPv4-Embedded IPv6 address using the Well-Known Prefix of RFC 6052, for home agents reached over an IPv4-only infrastructure. The Home Agent FQDN is used to look up A or AAAA records. Domain names are encoded as in Section 8 of RFC 3315.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of envelopes, and inside them go little notes: the home street, the home phone number, or the home's name. Each note must stay inside an envelope.

sections.title: How Clients Ask and Servers Answer
sections.content:
A mobile node may use a stateful exchange or a stateless one. With a stateful exchange it SHOULD include the same options in every message to the server. With a stateless exchange it MAY omit them from some exchanges but SHOULD reconfigure whenever it detects a change of attached network, and when an Information Request Timer option expires.

To ask for configuration, the client lists one or more of the three Home Network Information options in its Option Request Option (ORO). A client that does so MUST also request the Home Network Identifier FQDN, Home Network Prefix, Home Agent Address and Home Agent FQDN options. A client that wants the home network of a specific realm requests the Identified option and MUST include a Home Network ID FQDN option. A client with no preference SHOULD request the Unrestricted option and SHOULD NOT request the other two.

On the way back, the client MUST silently discard an Identified option whose FQDN does not match a request, any Home Network Information option with incomplete configuration, and any prefix, address or FQDN option that is not inside one of the three wrappers. If an option holds an IPv4-Embedded IPv6 address, the client may use it only to communicate over IPv4. Given several options of the same type, the node SHOULD choose the first one it can employ.

A relay agent that has the information MAY send the wrapper options to the server inside a Relay-Supplied Options option (RFC 6422). A server MAY keep a table of Home Network ID FQDNs and SHOULD include an Identified option for each match. Otherwise a server behaves as ordinary DHCPv6 does, and which clients get which Visited or Unrestricted options depends on operator configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The kid writes down which kinds of answers they want. The helper only gives back answers that match, and the kid throws away any note that is not in the right envelope.

sections.title: Using a Network Access Server
sections.content:
The complete procedure for home agent assignment among the mobile node, the NAS (Network Access Server), DHCP and AAA entities is described in RFC 5447. This RFC assumes the NAS is co-located with a DHCP relay agent or a DHCP server.

If the NAS is not co-located, the server may not receive the home network information from the NAS. It may then fail to provide information, or provide information that the administrator pre-configured or that it acquired by a mechanism this document does not describe.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk can only tell you where home is if it has been given that information by the person who checked you in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Delivery of the information relies on the same security as DHCP itself, and the options add no extra impact on DHCP security. Operators must separately make sure the information reaches the DHCP server securely, which is outside the scope of DHCP and these options.

Attackers could use the options to learn home agent addresses, which matters because brute-force scanning of IPv6 address space is not practical. Without protection on DHCP they could also feed wrong information to nodes. Nodes cannot be tricked into using wrong home agents, because communication with a home agent uses mutual authentication, and the authentic source of the information is that communication, not DHCP. The remaining risk is denial of service, if a node cannot connect to any home agent or picks one that is not the most preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could tell the kid a wrong address, but the real home will not let a stranger in, so the kid is safe. They might just waste time walking to the wrong door.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned seven DHCPv6 option codes in its dhcpv6-parameters registry: 49 OPTION_MIP6_HNIDF, 50 OPTION_MIP6_VDINF, 69 OPTION_MIP6_IDINF, 70 OPTION_MIP6_UDINF, 71 OPTION_MIP6_HNP, 72 OPTION_MIP6_HAA and 73 OPTION_MIP6_HAF.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new kind of note got its own number so everyone calls it the same thing.
